a.xlink:title: The cumulative height estimate is the input to partial summation.
mean-square bound
mean-square bound
Apply Chebyshev to the sum of the two nonnegative discrepancies.
Only the upper first-moment estimate (s=1) is used, through Jensen.
positive weighted asymptotic at tau=3/4
Apply the positive-measure spectral large sieve twice, using Hilbert-space duality.
window bound
high and holomorphic bounds

boundary error
Multiply the determinant-one matrices attached to the two Farey gaps.
Use the adjacent denominator relation to count long gaps.
determinant and denominator-sum identities
Apply the abstract large sieve with squared coefficient norm N_Q.
Apply the inequality to the multiset of ordered differences, including repetitions.
Set C=X and rewrite the two signs as signed frequencies.
estimate at delta=1
Reuse the proof of Corollary 3.3, replacing its numerical input by Proposition 3.4.
Use the two-frequency estimate as input to the weighted calculation.
Each shifted dyadic frequency block contributes at most X^-2(2^(j1+j2)X)^eta to the weighted height average of |a_Y(k)|^2.
Sum O(log^2 K) blocks, use Lemma 4.1, choose K=ceil(X^2), and eta=min(eps/6,1/2) to obtain (1.13).
A point in a product of short gaps bounds the distance.
For Q=floor(sqrt(X/2)), sup d_X<=sqrt(2)/Q<=4 X^-1/2.
Apply the one-dimensional tail bounds to dyadic product levels.
Estimate the measure where the product of adaptive orders is too large.
Integrate the distance-tail bound separately for 0<s<2, s=2, s>2; the two logarithms give the three stated orders.
Use the empty square (0,h)x(-h,0), h=1/(2 sqrt(X)), to get integral d_X^s >>_s X^(-1-s/2) for s>2.
Pack two disjoint empty squares at each rational pair with q1,q2<=X^(1/4)/4 and side 1/(2 sqrt(q1 q2 X)); obtain (c_2/(8X^2))(sum_{q<=X^(1/4)/4} phi(q)/q^2)^2.
uniform remainder estimate
total-weight identity at theta=0
Specialize the exact formula to L=tau Q^2.
The integral is positive throughout the stated tau range.
Low-spectrum Bessel kernel bounds supplies this part of the statement.
Identify negative frequencies with the opposite-sign sums.

For Q=floor(sqrt(X/2)), sup d_X<=sqrt(2)/Q<=4 X^-1/2.
For irrational x, Q^-2<=|I_Q(x)|<=Q^-1 and I_{Q+1}(x) subset I_Q(x). Defines the adaptive minimal order R_rho.
For irrational x, Q^-2<=|I_Q(x)|<=Q^-1 and I_{Q+1}(x) subset I_Q(x). Defines the adaptive minimal order R_rho.
Use the circular separation 1/(Q(Q-1)).
The strip [theta,Q^-2) x full-circle has no differences, including the diagonal, for 0<theta<Q^-2 and Q=floor(Y); let theta decrease to zero.
Pack two disjoint empty squares at each rational pair with q1,q2<=X^(1/4)/4 and side 1/(2 sqrt(q1 q2 X)); obtain (c_2/(8X^2))(sum_{q<=X^(1/4)/4} phi(q)/q^2)^2.

Removal of smoothing and comparison of bounds supplies this part of the statement.
Dyadic decomposition of the cumulative sum supplies this part of the statement.
Exceptional set uniform over real cutoffs supplies this part of the statement.
Apply the vector partial-summation calculation to the one-frequency vector.
Apply the same partial-summation calculation to the rectangular frequency vector.
Divisor reduction and treatment of the axes supplies this part of the statement.
The Fourier coefficients of the difference measure are squared absolute values.
Removing diagonal pairs changes probabilities by at most 1/N_Y.
Sum O(log^2 K) blocks, use Lemma 4.1, choose K=ceil(X^2), and eta=min(eps/6,1/2) to obtain (1.13).
Upper discrepancy bound supplies this part of the statement.
The strip [theta,Q^-2) x full-circle has no differences, including the diagonal, for 0<theta<Q^-2 and Q=floor(Y); let theta decrease to zero.
Lower discrepancy bound from an empty strip supplies this part of the statement.
Upper covering bound from Farey products supplies this part of the statement.
Integrate the distance-tail bound separately for 0<s<2, s=2, s>2; the two logarithms give the three stated orders.
The gap bounds and nesting control the least admissible order.
Integrate the distance-tail bound separately for 0<s<2, s=2, s>2; the two logarithms give the three stated orders.
Upper bounds for positive distance moments supplies this part of the statement.
Counting lower bound for positive moments supplies this part of the statement.
Combine the square packing and totient harmonic asymptotic to obtain integral d_X^2 >> X^-2(log X)^2 for large X; use counting for the remaining bounded range.
Use the empty square (0,h)x(-h,0), h=1/(2 sqrt(X)), to get integral d_X^s >>_s X^(-1-s/2) for s>2.
Pack two disjoint empty squares at each rational pair with q1,q2<=X^(1/4)/4 and side 1/(2 sqrt(q1 q2 X)); obtain (c_2/(8X^2))(sum_{q<=X^(1/4)/4} phi(q)/q^2)^2.
Supercritical lower bound from one empty square supplies this part of the statement.
Combine the square packing and totient harmonic asymptotic to obtain integral d_X^2 >> X^-2(log X)^2 for large X; use counting for the remaining bounded range.
Combine the square packing and totient harmonic asymptotic to obtain integral d_X^2 >> X^-2(log X)^2 for large X; use counting for the remaining bounded range.
Critical second-moment lower bound supplies this part of the statement.
Empty tangent disc and lower covering bound supplies this part of the statement.
Upper bound for negative moments supplies this part of the statement.
Lower bound for negative moments supplies this part of the statement.
Divergence of negative moments supplies this part of the statement.
Each shifted dyadic frequency block contributes at most X^-2(2^(j1+j2)X)^eta to the weighted height average of |a_Y(k)|^2.
Sum O(log^2 K) blocks, use Lemma 4.1, choose K=ceil(X^2), and eta=min(eps/6,1/2) to obtain (1.13).
For all s>0, integral d_X^s >= (1/2)(2 pi N_X)^(-s/2) >>_s X^-s.
For -2<s<0, union-bound meas{d_X<t}<=min(1,pi N_X t^2), then inverse layer-cake gives integral d_X^s <= 2/(s+2)(pi N_X)^(-s/2) <<_s X^-s.
The elementary count bounds Q(Q-1)N_Q by Q^4.
The reduced fractions are distinct frequencies and all coefficients have modulus one.
The pair calculation evaluates every off-diagonal term; no pair remains when L>=Q(Q-1).
Evaluate the coprime correction sum uniformly in tau.
Localization supplies a sharp interval at radius comparable to Q^2.
BRS, Lemma 4.3: Kuznetsov formula and local spectral large sieve.
BRS, Lemma 4.2: Twisted Bessel transform estimates.
BRS, Lemma 2.1: Koksma-Szusz base inequality.
DLMF, Equations (10.9.6) and (10.32.9): Integral representations of J and K Bessel functions.
IK, Corollary 11.12: Weil bound.
IK, Equation (1.81): Divisor small-power bound.
Xi, Equation (1.1): Selberg identity for integer arguments.
HW, Theorems 28 and 30: Adjacent Farey fractions.
HW, Theorem 271: Ramanujan-sum identity.
HW, Theorem 330: Summatory totient asymptotic.
MV, Lemma 2, equation (2.1); proof of Theorem 1: Cosecant bilinear inequality and endpoint argument.
Grafakos, Theorem 2.2.14 (4): Plancherel theorem.
Grafakos, Theorem 3.2.8: Poisson summation.
For real $N,X\ge1$, the height average of the second moment over $N\le\lvert n\rvert<2N$ is $\ll_\varepsilon (NX)^\varepsilon NX^2$. Both frequency signs are included.
For $N,X\ge1$ and $0<\delta\le1$, restricting the moduli to $(Y,(1+\delta)Y]$ gives the height-mean bound $\ll_\varepsilon (NX)^\varepsilon X^2\{N\delta+\min(1,N\delta^2X)\}$.

For $a,\kappa,\eta>0$ and $X\ge2$, outside a set of Lebesgue measure $O_{a,\kappa,\eta}(X^{1-\kappa+\eta})$, the bound $\mathcal K_2(N;Y)\le3NX^{2+\kappa}$ holds simultaneously for every real $1\le N\le X^a$.

For $X\ge2$, the height average of $\mathcal D_Y+\mathcal D_Y^*$ is $\ll_\varepsilon X^{-2+\varepsilon}$. Each discrepancy is at least $\lfloor Y\rfloor^{-2}$ for every $Y\ge2$. The supremum over rectangles is inside the average.
For $\kappa,\eta>0$ and $X\ge2$, both discrepancies are at most $X^{-2+\kappa}$ outside a set of Lebesgue measure $O_{\kappa,\eta}(X^{1-\kappa+\eta})$.

For $X\ge2$, the positive distance moments have orders $X^{-s}$ for $0<s<2$, $X^{-2}(\log X)^2$ for $s=2$, and $X^{-1-s/2}$ for $s>2$. The covering radius lies between $\tfrac12X^{-1/2}$ and $4X^{-1/2}$.

For integer $Q\ge2$, $1/2\le\tau<1$ and $L=\tau Q^2$, an exact sinc-squared weighted second moment isolates determinant-one Farey pairs. Its asymptotic is $LN_Q+(12\tau/\pi^2)I(\tau)Q^4+O(Q^3\log(2Q))$, uniformly in $\tau$, with $I(\tau)>0$.

For every sufficiently large integer $Q$, some symmetric interval with radius $T\asymp Q^2$ has a second-moment remainder whose absolute value is $\gg Q^4$. The constants are absolute; this is an existence statement for the interval.

Records the inverse Kuznetsov formula for both signs and the local spectral large sieve on a window of width $G$, for $N,T\ge1$ and $1\le G\le T$. The formula uses the signed measure $dm=\chi\,dm_0$; the large sieve uses positive $dm_0$.
Deduces a dual second-moment estimate $\ll_\eta F^2TG(TG+N)^{1+\eta}$ for a spectral-window integral with a multiplier bounded by $F$, for either sign.
Records the uniform-in-$r$ twisted Bessel estimates in the imaginary range $\lvert t\rvert\ge1$ and the holomorphic range $k\ge1$. The low imaginary spectrum is treated separately in Lemma 2.4.
For $\lvert t\rvert\le1$ and $Z>0$, both twisted transforms are $\ll_V1+\log^+(1/Z)$, uniformly in the real twist $r$.
For all integer $m,n$ and $c\ge1$, $\lvert S(m,n;c)\rvert\le(m,n,c)^{1/2}c^{1/2}\tau(c)$.
Expresses $S(m,n;c)$, for integer arguments, as a divisor sum of Kloosterman sums with one argument equal to one. The cumulative form is equation (2.6).
Consecutive fractions of Farey order $Q\ge1$ have determinant one and denominators whose sum exceeds $Q$.
For frequencies separated by $\lambda$ modulo one and any integer interval of length $H\ge1$, the absolute error from $H\sum_j\lvert y_j\rvert^2$ is at most $\lambda^{-1}\sum_j\lvert y_j\rvert^2$.

Bounds rectangular discrepancy of a nonempty finite sequence in $\mathbb T^2$ by a Fourier sum and a truncation term, allowing repeated points and closed or half-open arcs, including empty and full arcs.

For a fixed smooth compactly supported $W$, $C,N\ge1$ and real $r$, the second moment of the twisted smooth sums $B_\sigma(n,r)$ is $\ll_{\varepsilon,W}(NC(1+\lvert r\rvert))^\varepsilon(N+1+\lvert r\rvert)$.
Proves the moving-interval height mean at a base height $C\ge1$, with the factor $N\delta+\min(1,N\delta^2C)$. Theorem 1.2 is the corresponding formulation with signed frequencies.
For $N,X\ge1$, inserting the weight $1/c$ in the cumulative sums gives height-averaged second moment $\ll_\varepsilon(NX)^\varepsilon N$.

For $M,N,X\ge1$, the height-averaged second moment over $\lvert m\rvert\le M$, $\lvert n\rvert\le N$, excluding $(0,0)$, is $\ll_\varepsilon(MNX)^\varepsilon MNX^2$. Both coordinate axes are included.

With the weight $1/c$, the same frequency rectangle has height-averaged second moment $\ll_\varepsilon(MNX)^\varepsilon MN$. The proof of Corollary 3.3 is reused with Proposition 3.4 as the input estimate.
For $Y\ge2$ and integer $K\ge1$, controls $\mathcal D_Y$ by weighted squared Fourier coefficients and $1/K$, and proves $\mathcal D_Y^*\le\mathcal D_Y+1/N_Y$.
If integers $Q,R\ge1$ satisfy $2QR\le X$, every product of open consecutive Farey gaps of orders $Q$ and $R$ contains a lift of a point of $\mathcal P_X$.

For $0<\rho\le1$ and irrational $x$, controls the least Farey order $R_\rho(x)$ giving a gap of length at most $\rho$. It proves the range $\rho^{-1/2}\le R_\rho(x)\le2/\rho$ and a quadratic tail estimate.

Bounds the tail of $\rho R_\rho(x)R_\rho(y)$ by a quadratic decay times the smaller of two logarithmic factors, for $1\le z\le4/\rho$; above this range the tail is empty on irrational-coordinate pairs.
For $X\ge2$ and $t>0$, the measure of $\{d_X>t\}$ is $\ll [1+\min\{\log(2+Xt),\log(2+1/(Xt^2))\}]/(X^2t^2)$.
Gives an explicit arithmetic inequality in the denominators of the rational corner and the side lengths that makes two oppositely oriented open rectangles empty of lifts of $\mathcal P_X$.

For $X\ge2$ and $-2<s<0$, the distance moment has order $X^{-s}$. For $s\le-2$ it diverges. The three assertions use disc counting, the positive first-moment upper bound, and a local singularity, respectively.
For integer $Q\ge2$, $M\in\mathbb Z$ and integer $H\ge1$, the second moment over $M<n\le M+H$ differs from $HN_Q$ by at most $Q(Q-1)N_Q$.
For real $L\ge2$, the absolutely convergent Fourier series of $w(n/L)$ equals the triangular kernel $L(1-L\lVert\theta\rVert)_+$ for every real $\theta$.

For integer $Q\ge2$ and real $L\ge Q^2/2$, evaluates the weighted second moment as the diagonal term $LN_Q$ plus the contribution of determinant-one Farey pairs. The correction vanishes for $L\ge Q(Q-1)$.
For $1/2\le\tau<1$, reduces $I(\tau)$ to a one-dimensional integral and proves it is positive. On $[1/2,5/8]$ it gives the explicit lower bound $1/9000$.
Bounds the Schlaefli remainder integral and both low-spectrum kernels by $1+\log^+(1/x)$, then integrates over the fixed scaled support.
Records reality, interchange of the two arguments, and simultaneous sign reversal of Kloosterman sums. In particular, $S(-n,1;c)=S(n,-1;c)$.
Uses $\tau(n)\ll_\eta n^\eta$ for every $\eta>0$.
Sums Selberg's identity over the modulus to reduce $A_Y(m,n)$ to divisor-weighted sums $A_{Y/d}(mn/d^2,1)$ for $mn\ne0$. Terms with $d>Y$ vanish.
The Ramanujan-sum formula gives $\lvert A_Y(0,n)\rvert\le Y\tau(\lvert n\rvert)$ for $n\ne0$. Interchange of arguments covers the other axis.
The length of an adjacent Farey gap is $1/(qq')$ and lies between $Q^{-2}$ and $Q^{-1}$.
Increasing the Farey order adds fractions, so every new gap is contained in an old gap.
Distinct reduced fractions modulo one, with denominators at most $Q\ge2$, are separated by at least $1/[Q(Q-1)]$. The proof uses denominator arithmetic directly.
Writes the off-diagonal interval sum as a difference of two cosecant bilinear forms and bounds each by the Montgomery-Vaughan inequality.
Perturbs repeated points to distinct points and passes to limits. Monotone approximation then covers the stated arc conventions and degeneracies.
Applies Kuznetsov with a scalar of modulus one, separates low, holomorphic, and higher imaginary spectral ranges, and sums the window estimates by Minkowski.
Counts the moduli in a moving interval and the logarithmic height measure contributed by each modulus; the Weil and divisor bounds give the elementary mean-square estimate.
Constructs a smooth approximation to the moving interval and bounds its Mellin transform in terms of the interval length and the smoothing width.
The substitution $Y=C\exp(u)$ converts the height mean of the smooth sums to a Fourier Plancherel integral in the twist parameter.
Combines the twisted second moment, Mellin decay, and Plancherel to bound the smoothed height mean.
The smoothing changes at most two boundary moduli on the relevant height block. Bounds this error by Weil, then combines the spectral and elementary estimates to obtain the minimum in Lemma 3.2.
Decomposes the cumulative modulus sum into dyadic annuli and uses Minkowski. At most two contributing blocks lie below base height one; these are treated directly.
Applies Chebyshev on finitely many dyadic frequency blocks and covers each real interval $[N,2N)$ by two adjacent blocks. Their lengths sum to at most $3N$.
Applies partial summation coordinatewise and Minkowski to a finite vector of frequencies. An unweighted height mean then supplies the corresponding mean with weight $1/c$.
Uses cumulative Selberg, Cauchy-Schwarz, and divisor counting to apply Theorem 1.1. Treats base heights below one directly and handles the coordinate axes separately.
The normalized Fourier coefficient of the multiset of ordered differences is the squared absolute value of the coefficient of the original point set.
Splits the difference measure into distinct pairs and a mass $1/N_Y$ at zero. The resulting discrepancy change is at most $1/N_Y$.
Uses Proposition 3.4 and the cardinality comparison to bound each weighted dyadic frequency block. The blocks on the axes are retained; the origin is excluded.
Sums the frequency blocks, applies Lemma 4.1, and chooses the Fourier cutoff of order $X^2$ to prove the upper discrepancy bound.
The first coordinate determines the reduced denominator and then its unique modular inverse. Thus distinct points have distinct first coordinates, including the modulus-one origin.
Circular separation gives a strip containing no differences, including no diagonal difference. Letting its left endpoint approach zero gives the lower discrepancy bound.
Takes $Q=\lfloor\sqrt{X/2}\rfloor$ and uses a point in every product of Farey gaps to obtain the upper covering bound, including rational endpoints by closure.
Combines the Farey gap bounds with nesting and defines the least order at which the gap containing an irrational coordinate is short enough.
Expresses a positive distance moment as the integral of its tail by Tonelli's theorem.
Integrates the distance-tail estimate in the three ranges of $s$, using the already proved upper covering bound for the support cutoff.
The union of small discs around the $N_X$ points covers at most half the torus. This gives a lower moment bound of order $X^{-s}$ for every fixed $s>0$.
On an empty square, the distance to the point set is at least the distance to the boundary. Integrates this boundary distance explicitly.
One empty square of side $1/(2\sqrt X)$ gives the lower moment bound of order $X^{-1-s/2}$ for $s>2$.
Packs disjoint empty squares near rational pairs with small denominators. Their contributions produce the square of a harmonic totient sum.
Derives $\sum_{q\le y}\varphi(q)/q^2=(6/\pi^2)\log y+O(1)$ by the elementary Mobius formula and a harmonic-sum estimate.
Combines the disjoint-square packing with the totient sum to obtain the critical $X^{-2}(\log X)^2$ lower bound. The counting bound covers the remaining bounded range of heights.
Proves directly that a disc tangent at the origin contains no lift of the point set. This gives the lower covering bound independently of the empty-rectangle lemma.
Disc counting and the layer-cake identity for negative powers establish finiteness and the upper bound for $-2<s<0$.
Jensen's inequality and only the upper first-moment estimate in Theorem 1.6 give the lower bound for negative moments.
The origin belongs to the point set, so a local polar integral proves divergence for $s\le-2$.
The summatory totient estimate gives $N_X=(3/\pi^2)X^2+O(X\log(2X))$, hence $N_Y\asymp X^2$ for $X\le Y\le2X$. The discrepancy proof needs the lower bound for normalization.
The identity $N_X=\sum_{c\le X}\varphi(c)$ and $\varphi(c)\le c$ give $N_X\le X^2$ for $X\ge1$. This is sufficient for the distance counting arguments and the interval remainder bound.
Opens the Kloosterman sums to express $A_Q(n,1)$ using the $N_Q$ distinct reduced fractions as frequencies and inverse phases of modulus one as coefficients.
Compact support restricts the centered determinant residue to $+1$ or $-1$. The Chinese remainder theorem counts the pairs; their conjugate inverse phases give the cosine correction.
A uniform Lipschitz bound permits a Riemann-sum comparison on each sublattice. Mobius inversion produces the coprime main term and the $O(Q\log(2Q))$ error before multiplication by $2L$.

Combines the uniform sharp-interval remainder bound with the positive weighted correction. Abel summation and small variation near zero and in the far tail force a large remainder at radius comparable to $Q^2$.
Kuznetsov formula and local spectral large sieve; BRS, Lemma 4.3.
Twisted Bessel transform estimates; BRS, Lemma 4.2.
Koksma-Szusz base inequality; BRS, Lemma 2.1.
Integral representations of J and K Bessel functions; DLMF, Equations (10.9.6) and (10.32.9).
Weil bound; IK, Corollary 11.12.
Divisor small-power bound; IK, Equation (1.81).
Selberg identity for integer arguments; Xi, Equation (1.1).
Adjacent Farey fractions; HW, Theorems 28 and 30.
Ramanujan-sum identity; HW, Theorem 271.
Summatory totient asymptotic; HW, Theorem 330.
Cosecant bilinear inequality and endpoint argument; MV, Lemma 2, equation (2.1); proof of Theorem 1.
Plancherel theorem; Grafakos, Theorem 2.2.14 (4).
Poisson summation; Grafakos, Theorem 3.2.8.
